key_terms.meaning: A signal bandlimited to f<sub>m</sub> is fixed by samples taken at f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>m</sub>.
2f<sub>m</sub> samples/s, the lowest allowed sampling rate; the Nyquist interval is 1/(2f<sub>m</sub>).
f<sub>a</sub> = |f<sub>0</sub> − kf<sub>s</sub>| in 0 to f<sub>s</sub>/2: the false tone a component above f<sub>s</sub>/2 becomes.
Lowpass filter before the sampler; passes f<sub>m</sub>, stops by f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>m</sub>.
Droop of the message band by τ sinc(fτ) when each sample is held for τ.
The sample sets pulse height, pulse width (τ<sub>0</sub> + k<sub>w</sub>m) or pulse position.
Δ = 2V/L with L = 2ⁿ levels over −V to +V.
P<sub>q</sub> = Δ²/12; SQNR = 4.77 + 6.02n − 20 log(V/σ) dB, or 6.02n + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine.
Linear below |x|/V = 1/A, logarithmic above; A = 87.6.
R<sub>b</sub> = n f<sub>s</sub>; ideal minimum bandwidth R<sub>b</sub>/2.
(S/N)<sub>o</sub> = L²/(1 + 4L²P<sub>e</sub>).
G<sub>p</sub> = 10 log(σ²/σ<sub>e</sub>²); σ<sub>e</sub>² = 2σ²(1 − ρ) for x̂[n] = x̃[n − 1].
DPCM whose step (and often predictor) adapts to the short-term level; 32 kbit/s for speech.
One bit per sample; staircase moves ±Δ; R<sub>b</sub> = f<sub>s</sub>.
Staircase cannot follow the input; avoided when Δf<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2πfA.
Staircase hunting by ±Δ around a slow or flat input.
R<sub>b</sub> = (N n + S) f<sub>s</sub>; frame length 1/f<sub>s</sub>.
R<sub>b</sub> for NRZ and AMI; 2R<sub>b</sub> for RZ and Manchester.

takeaways: Sample at f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>m</sub> with a guard band; anything above f<sub>s</sub>/2 that reaches the sampler folds to |f − kf<sub>s</sub>| and cannot be removed later.
Flat-top sampling droops the band by sinc(fτ): 2.75 dB at 3.4 kHz for a full 125 µs hold, under 0.1 dB for a 25 µs pulse.
PAM, PWM and PPM carry the sample in height, width or position; constant-height PWM and PPM buy noise immunity with bandwidth.
Uniform quantization: P<sub>q</sub> = Δ²/12 and 6.02 dB per bit; a quiet signal loses 6 dB for every halving of its level.
μ-law and A-law companding hold an 8-bit SQNR near 34 to 38 dB over a 40 dB range of input levels, at the cost of about 12 dB at full scale.
PCM sends n f<sub>s</sub> bit/s (64 kbit/s for telephone speech) and needs at least half that in hertz; regeneration removes noise but not bit errors.
DPCM and ADPCM send prediction errors; with neighbour correlation 0.9 the gain is 7 dB, about one bit, and ADPCM halves the speech rate to 32 kbit/s.
Delta modulation is 1-bit DPCM: slope overload unless Δf<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2πfA, granular noise when Δ is large; ADM adapts Δ from the bits.
TDM frames last 1/f<sub>s</sub>; count every bit with (N n + S) f<sub>s</sub>: T1 is 1.544 Mbit/s and E1 2.048 Mbit/s.
Line codes trade DC, clock and bandwidth: NRZ is narrowest, Manchester is DC-free and self-clocking at twice the bandwidth, AMI is DC-free at NRZ bandwidth.
bank_note: Long answers usually follow the chain anti-aliasing filter → sampler → quantizer → encoder → multiplexer → line code, so keep each block’s number attached (f<sub>s</sub>, n, Δ, R<sub>b</sub>, SQNR). Most syllabi ask for the sampling theorem with a spectrum sketch, the Δ²/12 derivation, PCM, DPCM and delta modulation block diagrams with slope overload, and at least one bit-rate or TDM calculation; line-code waveforms with their spectra appear in fewer syllabi.

bank.q: State the sampling theorem for a lowpass signal and explain, with a spectrum sketch, why sampling below 2f<sub>m</sub> causes aliasing that cannot be removed later.
outline: Define f<sub>m</sub>, f<sub>s</sub>, T<sub>s</sub>; state f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>m</sub>, the Nyquist rate and interval
Spectrum of the sampled signal: copies of M(f) at every multiple of f<sub>s</sub>
If f<sub>s</sub> < 2f<sub>m</sub> the copies overlap; the overlap is the alias
A tone above f<sub>s</sub>/2 appears at |f − kf<sub>s</sub>|, with a numerical example
Once folded, no filter can separate the alias: hence the anti-aliasing filter

answer.text: Statement. A signal m(t) whose spectrum M(f) is zero for |f| > fm is determined completely by its samples m(nTs) if the sampling rate fs = 1/Ts ≥ 2fm. The minimum rate 2fm is the Nyquist rate and the largest interval 1/(2fm) is the Nyquist interval.

Ideal sampling. Model the sampler as multiplication by an impulse train: s(t) = m(t) Σ δ(t − nTs) = Σ m(nTs) δ(t − nTs). The impulse train is periodic with period Ts; all its Fourier-series coefficients equal 1/Ts, so its transform is fs Σ δ(f − kfs).
Spectrum of the samples. Multiplication in time is convolution in frequency, so S(f) = fs Σ M(f − kfs). Sketch: the baseband triangle from −fm to fm, and identical triangles centred at ±fs, ±2fs, … .

Condition for no overlap. The copy at fs starts at fs − fm. It clears the baseband when fs − fm ≥ fm, that is fs ≥ 2fm. The gap fs − 2fm is the guard band, and a lowpass filter of gain Ts with its cutoff anywhere from fm to fs − fm returns M(f) exactly.

Overlap when fs < 2fm. The copy at fs now reaches below fm, so its upper part lies on top of the baseband. Seen from the baseband, every component above fs/2 folds about fs/2 and appears at fa = |f − kfs|, with k chosen so that 0 ≤ fa ≤ fs/2.
Numerical example. Take x(t) = 2 cos(2π·3000t), so fm = 3 kHz and the Nyquist rate is 6 kHz.

head: f<sub>s</sub>
lines of S(f) up to 13 kHz
inside 0 to f<sub>s</sub>/2
output tone

answer.text: Why the alias cannot be removed. At fs = 5 kHz, cos(2π·3000n/5000) = cos(2πn − 2π·2000n/5000) = cos(2π·2000n/5000): the samples of the 3 kHz tone are exactly those of a 2 kHz tone. The sample sequence carries no trace of which one was sent, so no filter, however good, can undo the fold. A real 2 kHz component of the message would be indistinguishable from it.

The cure. Limit the input before the sampler with an anti-aliasing filter that passes fm and stops everything from fs − fm up, and choose fs above 2fm so that the filter has a guard band to roll off in. Telephony uses fm = 3.4 kHz with fs = 8 kHz, a 1.2 kHz guard band.
Closing check. At fs = 5 kHz the folding frequency is 2.5 kHz; 3 kHz lies 0.5 kHz above it and reappears 0.5 kHz below it, at 2 kHz, which matches |3 − 5| = 2 kHz.

bank.q: Compare PAM, PWM and PPM on the message-carrying parameter, pulse amplitude, bandwidth, power and noise immunity, and explain how each is generated.
outline: PAM: amplitude varies; sample-and-hold; natural and flat-top forms
PWM: width varies, amplitude fixed; comparator with a sawtooth
PPM: position varies; from the PWM trailing edge with a monostable
Bandwidth order PAM < PWM < PPM and the reason
Noise immunity of constant-height pulses; PWM wastes power
A numerical illustration

answer.text: Common frame. All three send one pulse per sampling period Ts = 1/fs, with fs ≥ 2fm; they differ in which pulse property follows the sample m(nTs).

PAM generation. A sample-and-hold circuit samples m(t) every Ts and holds the value for τ (flat-top PAM); a switch gated by a pulse train gives natural PAM, whose top follows m(t). The flat-top spectrum is fs τ sinc(fτ) Σ M(f − kfs): copies of M(f) shaped by the pulse, which causes the aperture effect.

PWM generation. Compare m(t) with a sawtooth of period Ts in a comparator. The output is high from the start of each period until the sawtooth passes the message, so the leading edge is fixed and the trailing edge moves: τn = τ0 + kw m(nTs).

PPM generation. Differentiate the PWM wave, keep the negative (trailing-edge) spikes, and let each trigger a monostable that outputs a short pulse of fixed width. That gives one pulse per period, displaced from its nominal position in proportion to the sample.
Numerical illustration. With fs = 10 kHz, τ0 = 50 µs and kw = 10 µs/V, the samples +2, +1, −1, −3 V give:
Comparison.

head: Property
PAM
PWM
PPM
rows: highest: narrow pulses with fast edges

answer.text: Why the bandwidth order. PWM and PPM carry the message in edge timing, so the edges must be much sharper than the smallest width change; a rise time tr needs about 1/(2tr) of bandwidth. For example, to resolve 1 µs shifts the edges need tr ≤ 0.5 µs, which is about 1 MHz, while 20 µs PAM pulses need only about 25 to 50 kHz.

Why the noise order. A constant-height pulse can be sliced at half height, so amplitude noise affects it only through the small timing jitter it causes on the edge; PAM puts the message in the height, so the noise adds directly to the recovered sample.
Closing check. In the table every PWM width lies between 0 and 100 µs, and each PPM shift equals the width change from 50 µs: 70 − 50 = +20 µs, 20 − 50 = −30 µs.

bank.q: Derive the quantization noise power Δ²/12 of a uniform quantizer and hence the SQNR for a full-scale sinusoid. Tabulate the SQNR for 6 to 10 bits.
outline: Error e uniform in −Δ/2 to Δ/2 with density 1/Δ
Mean square error = Δ²/12
Signal power of a full-scale sine V²/2
Δ = 2V/2ⁿ gives SQNR = 1.5 × 2²ⁿ = 6.02n + 1.76 dB
General form 4.77 + 6.02n − 20 log(V/σ)
Assumptions: fine steps, no overload

answer.text: Quantizer. An n-bit uniform quantizer covers −V to +V with L = 2ⁿ levels, so the step is Δ = 2V/L. Each sample x is replaced by the nearest level q(x); the error e = q(x) − x lies in −Δ/2 ≤ e ≤ Δ/2 as long as |x| ≤ V.

Assumption. For a busy signal and small Δ, the sample falls anywhere within a step with equal likelihood, so e is uniformly distributed with probability density p(e) = 1/Δ on −Δ/2 to Δ/2. Its mean is zero by symmetry.
Noise power.
answer.pre:
P<sub>q</sub> = E[e²] = ∫ e² p(e) de   (from −Δ/2 to +Δ/2)
    = (1/Δ) [e³/3] from −Δ/2 to +Δ/2
    = (1/Δ) (Δ³/24 + Δ³/24)
    = Δ²/12

answer.text: Full-scale sine. For x(t) = V sin(ωt) the mean-square value is Px = V²/2. Then SQNR = (V²/2)/(Δ²/12) = 6V²/Δ². With Δ = 2V/2ⁿ, Δ² = 4V²/2²ⁿ and SQNR = 6V² · 2²ⁿ/(4V²) = 1.5 × 2²ⁿ.
In decibels. 10 log(1.5 × 2²ⁿ) = 10 log 1.5 + 20n log 2 = 1.76 + 6.02n dB. Each extra bit multiplies L by 2 and the SQNR by 4, which is 6.02 dB.
Any signal. For a signal of rms value σ, SQNR = 3L²σ²/V², or 4.77 + 6.02n − 20 log(V/σ) dB. For the sine V/σ = √2 gives back 1.76 dB; speech held to peaks of 4σ gives 6.02n − 7.27 dB.
Table.

Limits of the result. It assumes no overload (|x| ≤ V), a step small enough for the uniform-error model, and a full-scale sine. A sine at half amplitude loses 6.02 dB; clipping beyond ±V is extra distortion not included in Δ²/12.
Closing check. For 8 bits and ±1 V: Δ = 7.8125 mV, Pq = 5.086 × 10⁻⁶ V², Px = 0.5 V², ratio 98 304, which is 49.93 dB, matching 6.02 × 8 + 1.76 = 49.92 dB.

bank.q: Explain a PCM system with a block diagram, and define bit rate, bit duration and quantization error. Work the numbers for telephone speech.
outline: Blocks: anti-aliasing filter, sampler, quantizer, encoder, channel with regenerative repeaters, decoder, reconstruction filter
f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>m</sub>; L = 2ⁿ; R<sub>b</sub> = n f<sub>s</sub>; T<sub>b</sub> = 1/R<sub>b</sub>
Quantization error within ±Δ/2 and its power Δ²/12
Bandwidth R<sub>b</sub>/2 (ideal) or R<sub>b</sub> (NRZ first null)
Regeneration and why noise does not accumulate

answer.text: Block diagram. Draw, left to right: m(t) → anti-aliasing LPF (cutoff fm) → sampler (fs) → quantizer (L levels) → encoder (n bits) → line, with regenerative repeaters every few kilometres → regenerator at the receiver → decoder → reconstruction LPF → m̂(t). A clock at Rb drives the encoder and decoder.

Transmitter blocks. The LPF removes content above fm so that sampling at fs ≥ 2fm does not alias. The quantizer rounds each sample to the nearest of L = 2ⁿ levels (companded for speech). The encoder writes the level number as an n-bit code word.

Channel and receiver. Each regenerative repeater equalizes the pulses, recovers the clock, decides 0 or 1 at mid-bit and sends a fresh pulse, so the noise of one span does not pass to the next. The decoder converts each word back to its level, and the LPF smooths the staircase of levels into the output waveform.
Definitions. Bit rate Rb = n fs bit/s. Bit duration Tb = 1/Rb. Quantization error e = q(x) − x, bounded by ±Δ/2 with Δ = 2V/L, and of mean-square value Δ²/12.
Telephone numbers. For speech bandlimited to 3.4 kHz, sampled at 8 kHz with 8 bits on a ±1 V range:

Why PCM. Noise is removed at every repeater, so quality depends on the bit-error rate, not the route length; the signal can be stored, switched, encrypted and multiplexed as bits; SQNR is chosen by n. The price is bandwidth: n times the message bandwidth at the Nyquist rate.
Effect of bit errors. With error probability Pe, (S/N)o = L²/(1 + 4L²Pe). For n = 8 and Pe = 10⁻⁶ this is 65 536/1.262 = 51 924, or 47.2 dB, close to the error-free 48.2 dB.
Closing check. Rb × Tb = 64 000 × 15.625 µs = 1, and 8 bits × 15.625 µs = 125 µs = Ts: one code word fills exactly one sampling interval.

bank.q: Explain DPCM and ADPCM with block diagrams, and show with numbers how prediction reduces the bits needed for speech.
outline: Prediction from past reconstructed samples; e[n] = x[n] − x̂[n]
Quantize and send e[n]; receiver adds the same prediction
Local decoder in the transmitter: why both ends use x̃
Prediction gain 10 log(σ²/σ<sub>e</sub>²); bits saved ≈ G<sub>p</sub>/6.02
ADPCM: step and predictor adapt from past codes; 32 kbit/s

answer.text: Idea. Neighbouring speech samples are strongly correlated, so a prediction x̂[n] from past samples is close to x[n]. DPCM sends only the prediction error e[n] = x[n] − x̂[n], which has a much smaller spread and so needs fewer levels for the same step.

Transmitter. x[n] and x̂[n] enter a subtractor; e[n] is quantized to q[n] and encoded in N bits. A local decoder adds q[n] to x̂[n] to form x̃[n] = x̂[n] + q[n], which goes into the predictor for the next sample.
Receiver. The decoder recovers q[n]; an adder forms x̃[n] = x̂[n] + q[n] with an identical predictor fed from its own output; a lowpass filter smooths x̃.

Why the closed loop. The receiver has only q[n], so it can only compute x̃. Predicting from x̃ at both ends keeps the two predictors identical, and the output error is just e[n] − q[n], one quantization error that does not accumulate. Predicting from x (open loop) would let the receiver drift.
Trace. Predictor x̂[n] = x̃[n − 1], 3-bit quantizer of step 0.5 V (levels ±0.25 … ±1.75 V), x̃[−1] = 0:

Prediction gain. For variance σ² and neighbour correlation ρ, the simple predictor gives σe² = 2σ²(1 − ρ). With σ² = 1 V² and ρ = 0.9: σe² = 0.2 V² and Gp = 10 log(1/0.2) = 6.99 dB. The best coefficient a = ρ gives σ²(1 − ρ²) = 0.19 V², 7.21 dB.
Bits saved. Every 6.02 dB of gain is worth one bit, so 6.99 dB saves 6.99/6.02 = 1.16 bits per sample: DPCM with 7 bits matches 8-bit PCM, 56 kbit/s instead of 64 kbit/s at 8 kHz.

ADPCM. The step Δ[n] is scaled up after large codes and down after small ones, and the predictor coefficients may adapt too; both are computed from past codes, so no side information is sent. This adds several dB more, and the ITU-T G.726 coder sends 4 bits at 8 kHz: 32 kbit/s for toll-quality speech, half of PCM.
Closing check. In the trace every |x − x̃| ≤ 0.25 V = Δ/2 although x reaches 2.4 V, outside the ±1.75 V quantizer range: the quantizer only ever sees differences up to 1.1 V.

bank.q: Describe delta modulation with a block diagram, and define slope overload and granular noise with the condition to avoid overload.
outline: 1-bit coder: comparator, sampler, integrator in feedback
Staircase moves ±Δ per sample; R<sub>b</sub> = f<sub>s</sub>
Slope overload and the condition Δf<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2πfA
Granular noise and the step-size trade-off
ADM as the remedy

answer.text: Transmitter. Draw x(t) into a comparator whose other input is the staircase x̃; the comparator output is sampled at fs to give one bit b[n]; the bit drives an integrator (accumulator) that adds +Δ for a 1 and −Δ for a 0, closing the loop.
Receiver. An identical integrator rebuilds the staircase from the bits, and a lowpass filter at fm smooths it. Since there is one bit per sample, Rb = fs and no word framing is needed.
Rule. b[n] = 1 if x[n] ≥ x̃[n − 1], else 0; then x̃[n] = x̃[n − 1] ± Δ. DM is DPCM with a 1-bit quantizer and the prediction x̃[n − 1].

Slope overload. The staircase can change by at most Δ per sample, a slope of Δfs. For x(t) = A sin(2πft) the steepest slope is 2πfA, so overload is avoided only if Δfs ≥ 2πfA. Otherwise the staircase lags and a long run of equal bits appears.

Example. A = 2 V, f = 1 kHz, Δ = 0.1 V, fs = 32 kHz: the input slope is 2π × 1000 × 2 = 12 566 V/s and the staircase slope 0.1 × 32 000 = 3200 V/s, so the coder overloads. It needs fs ≥ 12 566/0.1 = 125.7 kHz, or Δ ≥ 12 566/32 000 = 0.393 V.

Granular noise. On a flat or slow input the staircase hunts ±Δ around it, giving a noise of peak about Δ. A large Δ cures overload but raises granular noise; a small Δ does the opposite. So a fixed-step DM must compromise.
Remedy. Adaptive DM multiplies Δ by K > 1 after a run of equal bits and divides it after alternating bits, between set limits; the receiver applies the same rule to the same bits.
Closing check. With Δ = 0.393 V and 32 kHz, Δfs = 12 576 V/s ≥ 12 566 V/s, so the overload condition is just met.

bank.q: A speech signal bandlimited to 3.4 kHz is sampled at 8 kHz and coded with 8-bit uniform PCM. Find the bit rate, the ideal minimum and NRZ first-null bandwidths, and the SQNR for a full-scale sinusoid and for speech with peaks at 4σ.
outline: Check the sampling rate against the Nyquist rate
R<sub>b</sub> = n f<sub>s</sub> = 64 kbit/s
B<sub>min</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2 = 32 kHz; NRZ first null at R<sub>b</sub> = 64 kHz
SQNR = 1.5 × 2¹⁶ → 49.9 dB

answer.text: Sampling check. Nyquist rate = 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 kHz. fs = 8 kHz exceeds it, so there is no aliasing; the guard band is 8 − 6.8 = 1.2 kHz and the anti-aliasing filter must stop by 8 − 3.4 = 4.6 kHz.
Bit rate. Rb = n fs = 8 × 8000 = 64 000 bit/s = 64 kbit/s; Tb = 1/64 000 s = 15.6 µs.

Bandwidths. With ideal Nyquist (sinc) pulses the minimum bandwidth is Rb/2 = 32 kHz. With rectangular polar NRZ pulses the PSD is V²Tb sinc²(fTb), whose first null is at 1/Tb = Rb = 64 kHz; about 90 % of the power lies below it. A raised-cosine pulse with roll-off α needs (1 + α)Rb/2, for example 48 kHz at α = 0.5.
Levels and step. L = 2⁸ = 256. On a ±1 V range Δ = 2/256 = 7.8125 mV and Pq = Δ²/12 = 5.086 × 10⁻⁶ V².

Speech. Speech is not a full-scale sine; with peaks held at four times the rms value, SQNR = 4.77 + 6.02 × 8 − 20 log 4 = 4.77 + 48.16 − 12.04 = 40.9 dB. A quieter talker loses a further 6 dB per halving of level, which is why telephony companding is used.
Summary.
Closing check. The two SQNRs differ by 49.9 − 40.9 = 9.0 dB, which is 20 log(4/√2) = 9.03 dB, the difference between a loading factor of 4 and of √2.

bank.q: Sixteen PCM channels, each sampled at 8 kHz with 8 bits per sample, are time division multiplexed. Find the frame duration, slot width, bit duration and line rate; then add one sync bit per frame and a one-bit guard time per slot and recompute.
outline: Frame = 1/f<sub>s</sub> = 125 µs
Bits per frame 16 × 8 = 128; R<sub>b</sub> = 1.024 Mbit/s
Slot 7.8125 µs; bit 0.977 µs
With a sync bit and a 1-bit guard per slot: 145 bits, 1.16 Mbit/s
Why the guard and sync bits are needed

answer.text: Frame. Every channel must be sampled at 8 kHz, so one frame (one sample of each channel) lasts Tf = 1/8000 s = 125 µs, independent of the number of channels.
Plain frame. Bits per frame = N n = 16 × 8 = 128. Rb = 128 × 8000 = 1 024 000 bit/s = 1.024 Mbit/s. Slot = 125/16 = 7.8125 µs; bit = 125/128 = 0.977 µs.

Why add bits. The receiver must find the frame start, so at least one sync bit per frame (in practice a pattern spread over several frames) is needed. A guard time between slots absorbs clock jitter and pulse spreading so that a late or early decision does not read the neighbouring slot.
Frame with sync and guard. Each slot now holds 8 data bits plus 1 guard bit, and one sync bit closes the frame: 16 × 9 + 1 = 145 bits.
Working of the last row. Rb = 145 × 8000 = 1 160 000 bit/s; Tb = 125 µs/145 = 0.862 µs; slot = 9 × 0.862 = 7.76 µs, of which the guard is 0.862 µs. The overhead is 17/145 = 11.7 % of the line.

How much guard. The guard must exceed the worst timing error between the transmitter and receiver clocks over one frame plus the pulse spreading of the channel. One bit (0.86 µs) tolerates a timing error of up to about ±0.4 µs around the slot centre; a well-locked receiver needs less, which is why telephone systems such as E1 use no guard bits at all.
Minimum bandwidth. With Nyquist pulses Bmin = Rb/2: 512 kHz for the plain frame and 580 kHz with the overhead. As PAM-TDM instead, 16 × 8000 = 128 000 pulses/s would need only 64 kHz.
Closing check. 16 slots × 7.76 µs + 0.862 µs sync = 124.1 + 0.86 = 125.0 µs, one frame.

bank.q: A message bandlimited to 3 kHz is sampled at 8 kHz. Interferers at 5.5 kHz and 9 kHz, each 20 dB above the message, reach the sampler. Find their aliases, specify the anti-aliasing filter, and find the Butterworth order that brings them 40 dB below the message. How does raising f<sub>s</sub> to 12 kHz change the filter?
outline: f<sub>s</sub>/2 = 4 kHz; aliases at |f − kf<sub>s</sub>|
Both aliases fall in the message band
Filter: pass 3 kHz, stop by f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>m</sub> = 5 kHz
Required attenuation 60 dB; Butterworth order from 10 log(1 + (f/f<sub>c</sub>)²ᴺ)
Higher f<sub>s</sub> widens the guard band and lowers the order

answer.text: Aliases. Folding frequency fs/2 = 4 kHz. 5.5 kHz → |5.5 − 8| = 2.5 kHz. 9 kHz → |9 − 8| = 1 kHz. Both lie inside the 0 to 3 kHz message band, so after sampling they are indistinguishable from message content.

Where the filter must stop. A component at f folds to fs − f, which falls inside 0 to 3 kHz when f ≥ 8 − 3 = 5 kHz. So the filter passes 3 kHz and must attenuate fully from 5 kHz upward; the 5.5 kHz interferer is the nearest one.
Attenuation needed. The interferers are 20 dB above the message and must end 40 dB below it, so the filter needs 20 + 40 = 60 dB of attenuation at 5.5 kHz (and more is easy at 9 kHz).

Butterworth order. A Butterworth lowpass with its 3 dB edge at fc = 3 kHz attenuates 10 log[1 + (f/fc)²ᴺ] dB. Setting 60 dB at 5.5 kHz: (5.5/3)²ᴺ ≥ 10⁶ − 1, so N ≥ 6/(2 log 1.833) = 6/0.5264 = 11.4, hence N = 12.

Raising fs. At 12 kHz the filter must stop from 12 − 3 = 9 kHz. The 5.5 kHz interferer now folds to 6.5 kHz, outside the message band, and is removed by the reconstruction filter; the 9 kHz one folds to 3 kHz, the band edge. With 60 dB needed at 9 kHz, N ≥ 6/(2 log 3) = 6.29, so N = 7.
Trade-off. A faster sampler buys a simpler analog filter (order 7 instead of 12) at the cost of 1.5 times the bit rate in a PCM system.
Closing check. N = 12 at 5.5 kHz: 10 log(1 + 1.833²⁴) = 63.2 dB ≥ 60 dB; N = 11 would give 57.9 dB, short of 60 dB.

bank.q: For an 8-bit PCM system with a full-scale range of ±2 V, find the step size, the maximum quantization error, the noise power and the SQNR for a full-scale sine, and compare with a 12-bit system at 8 kHz sampling.
outline: P<sub>q</sub> = Δ²/12 = 2.03 × 10⁻⁵ V²
SQNR = 49.9 dB
12 bits: Δ = 0.977 mV, P<sub>q</sub> = 7.95 × 10⁻⁸ V², 74.0 dB
4 more bits = 24.1 dB for 32 kbit/s more

answer.text: 8-bit step. L = 2⁸ = 256 over a range of 2V = 4 V, so Δ = 4/256 = 0.015625 V = 15.6 mV.
Maximum error. Inside the range the error never exceeds Δ/2 = 7.8 mV.
SQNR. A full-scale sine of peak 2 V has Px = 2²/2 = 2 V². SQNR = 2/2.035 × 10⁻⁵ = 98 304, which is 49.9 dB, the same as for any range: SQNR depends on n and on the loading, not on V.
Comparison.

What the extra bits buy. Four more bits divide Δ by 16, so the noise power falls by 256 and SQNR rises by 10 log 256 = 24.1 dB, 6.02 dB per bit. The cost is 1.5 times the bit rate and bandwidth. A quiet talker 30 dB down still gets 44 dB with 12 bits but only 20 dB with 8, which is the same problem companding solves.

bank.q: Sketch the waveforms of NRZ-L, polar RZ, Manchester and differential Manchester for the bits 1 0 1 1 0 0 1, and compare the codes on DC content, clock recovery and bandwidth, with first nulls at 1 kbit/s.
outline: NRZ-L: level held for the whole bit
Polar RZ: pulse in the first half, zero in the second
Manchester: centre transition, state the convention
Differential Manchester: data in the start-of-bit transition
DC: average levels of this word and PSD at f = 0
Clock: transitions per bit; no spectral line in polar codes
Bandwidth: first nulls R<sub>b</sub> and 2R<sub>b</sub>

answer.text: Conventions. Bit time Tb, levels ±V. NRZ-L: 1 = +V, 0 = −V. Polar RZ: 1 = +V then 0, 0 = −V then 0. Manchester (IEEE 802.3): 1 = low-to-high, 0 = high-to-low. Differential Manchester: always a centre transition; a 0 has a transition at the start of the bit, a 1 has none.
Waveforms. Drawn bit by bit:

svg.aria: Waveforms of the bits 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 in NRZ-L, polar RZ, Manchester and differential Manchester.

answer.text: Levels in each half-bit.

DC content. NRZ-L for this word averages (4 − 3)V/7 = +0.14V and polar RZ +0.07V: their DC follows the data, and their PSDs, V²Tb sinc²(fTb) and (V²Tb/4) sinc²(fTb/2), peak at f = 0. Both Manchester codes average 0 in every bit, so they have no DC whatever the data and pass through transformers.

Clock recovery. NRZ-L has a transition only when the data changes (4 here in 7 bits), and none at all in a long run, so the clock can drift. Polar RZ has an edge in every bit. Manchester and differential Manchester have a guaranteed centre transition in every bit, so they are self-clocking. None of these polar codes has a discrete spectral line at Rb for random data; the receiver creates one by rectifying or squaring the signal and then filters it with a PLL.
Bandwidth at 1 kbit/s. Tb = 1 ms.

Polarity. If the two wires are swapped, NRZ-L and Manchester read every bit inverted; differential Manchester reads the same bits, because it carries data in whether a transition occurs, not in its direction.

Choice. NRZ for the least bandwidth when scrambling guarantees transitions; Manchester or differential Manchester where DC must be blocked and the clock must come from the data, as in 10 Mbit/s Ethernet, at twice the bandwidth.
Closing check. Manchester transitions in this word: 7 at the bit centres plus 2 at boundaries between equal bits (1 1 and 0 0), 9 in all; NRZ-L has only 4, at the data changes 1→0, 0→1, 1→0 and 0→1.

bank.q: Compare PCM, DPCM, ADPCM and delta modulation for telephone speech on bit rate, SNR, complexity and behaviour on quiet passages, and recommend one for a trunk line and one for a low-cost voice link.
outline: PCM: 64 kbit/s; 6.02 dB per bit; companding for quiet talkers
DPCM: prediction gain about 7 dB saves about one bit
ADPCM: 32 kbit/s at comparable quality
DM: 1 bit at a high f<sub>s</sub>; SNR = 3f<sub>s</sub>³/(8π²f²W); slope overload and granular noise
Complexity: DM < PCM < DPCM < ADPCM
Recommendation with reasons

answer.text: Common basis. Speech bandlimited to W = 3.4 to 4 kHz. Compare the four at their usual operating points and with the same test signal where a number is given.

PCM. 8 bits at 8 kHz, 64 kbit/s. Uniform 8-bit SQNR is 49.9 dB for a full-scale sine and 40.9 dB for speech at 4σ, falling 6 dB per halving of level; μ-law or A-law companding holds about 34 to 38 dB over a 40 dB range. Each sample is coded on its own, so a bit error affects one sample.

DPCM. With neighbour correlation ρ = 0.9 the prediction gain is 6.99 dB (7.21 dB with the best coefficient), worth 1.16 bits: 7 bits at 8 kHz, 56 kbit/s, give PCM-like quality. A bit error now enters the predictor and lingers for a few samples.

ADPCM. Adapting the step to the talker level and the predictor to the spectrum adds more gain, so 4 bits at 8 kHz (32 kbit/s, ITU-T G.726) give quality close to 64 kbit/s PCM. Quiet passages get a small step, so granular noise follows the level.
Delta modulation. 1 bit per sample at a high rate. For a tone at the largest amplitude that avoids overload, SNR = 3fs³/(8π²f²W). With f = 1 kHz and W = 4 kHz:

Reading the DM numbers. Doubling the bit rate adds only 9 dB to DM, while one more PCM bit at 8 kHz adds 6 dB for just 8 kbit/s. At 64 kbit/s, DM gives about 34 dB against 49.9 dB for PCM. Fixed DM also suffers slope overload on loud, fast speech and granular noise on quiet passages; ADM (CVSD) removes much of both.
Summary.
Complexity order. DM (comparator, integrator, clock) < PCM (quantizer and encoder) < DPCM (adds a predictor and local decoder) < ADPCM (adds step and predictor adaptation).

Recommendation. A trunk line carrying many calls should use companded PCM, or ADPCM where capacity matters: they give toll quality, and ADPCM doubles the calls per line. A low-cost voice link (intercom, toy, simple radio) should use ADM: one-bit hardware, no framing, graceful behaviour under bit errors, acceptable quality at 32 to 64 kbit/s.
Closing check. From 32 to 64 kbit/s the DM SNR rises 34.0 − 24.9 = 9.0 dB, which is 10 log 2³ = 9.03 dB, as the fs³ law predicts.

bank.q: Explain why companding is used in speech PCM. Draw the μ-law and A-law compression curves, and compare the SQNR of uniform and μ-law 8-bit PCM for weak and strong talkers.
outline: Uniform PCM loses 6 dB per halving of level, so weak talkers suffer
Compressor, uniform quantizer, expander; small signals get fine steps
μ-law formula, μ = 255; A-law formula, A = 87.6; the curves
SQNR table against level for uniform and μ-law
μ-law large-signal SQNR ≈ 3L²/[ln(1 + μ)]² = 38 dB
Costs: about 12 dB at full scale, non-compatible laws, overload still possible

answer.text: The problem. Uniform quantization gives the same Δ²/12 noise to every sample, so SQNR is proportional to signal power. Talkers differ by 30 dB or more, and speech is small most of the time, so a quiet talker on 8-bit uniform PCM would get only 10 to 20 dB.

Companding. A compressor y = C(x) before a uniform quantizer lifts small inputs; an expander C⁻¹ after the decoder restores them. The effective step at an input x is Δ/C′(x): fine near zero, coarse near full scale. With a logarithmic C, the noise grows in proportion to the signal and SQNR becomes nearly independent of level.
μ-law. y = ln(1 + μ|x|/V)/ln(1 + μ) with odd symmetry, μ = 255 (North America, Japan). Slope at zero 255/ln 256 = 46.0: small signals see a step 46 times finer, a 33.3 dB gain.
A-law. y = A(|x|/V)/(1 + ln A) for |x|/V ≤ 1/A, and [1 + ln(A|x|/V)]/(1 + ln A) above, A = 87.6 (Europe, India). Slope at zero 87.6/5.473 = 16.0, a 24.1 dB gain.
Curves. Both rise steeply from zero and bend over; sample values: μ-law 0.01 → 0.229, 0.1 → 0.591, 0.5 → 0.876; A-law 0.01 → 0.160, 0.1 → 0.579, 0.5 → 0.873.

svg.aria: Mu-law and A-law compression curves rising steeply from zero and bending over, compared with the straight uniform line.

answer.text: SQNR against level. 8 bits on ±V, sine inputs, μ-law values from the fine-step formula:
Large-signal limit. When μ|x| ≫ V, μ-law SQNR ≈ 3L²/[ln(1 + μ)]² = 3 × 65 536/30.75 = 6394, or 38.1 dB, independent of level.

Evaluation. Companding trades about 12 dB at full scale (49.9 against 38.0 dB) for a 40 dB range over which SQNR stays within 4 dB of 38 dB; for speech that trade is worth it, because a strong talker does not need 50 dB while a weak one badly needs 30. The cost: a compressor and expander (today a lookup table), the two incompatible laws needing conversion on international calls, and no protection against overload beyond ±V. Idle-channel noise is reduced by the fine steps near zero but not removed.

Closing check. At −40 dB the uniform quantizer gives 49.9 − 40 = 9.9 dB, and μ-law improves it by 34.4 − 9.9 = 24.5 dB; the improvement is below the 33.3 dB small-signal limit because a −40 dB sine still reaches into the bent part of the curve.

bank.q: Design a TDM-PCM system for 30 telephone channels: choose the sampling rate, bits per sample, frame structure with synchronization and signalling, and line rate, and discuss timing, guard time and the line code. Compare your design with E1.
outline: f<sub>s</sub> = 8 kHz, frame 125 µs, 8 bits per sample with A-law
30 speech slots + frame alignment slot + signalling slot = 32 slots
256 bits per frame; R<sub>b</sub> = 2.048 Mbit/s; slot 3.91 µs; bit 0.488 µs
Frame alignment word and false-lock probability
Clock recovery, jitter and guard time
Line code HDB3 and bandwidth
Comparison with a minimal 30 × 8 + 1 frame

answer.text: Sampling. Speech is bandlimited to 3.4 kHz, so fs = 8 kHz (guard band 1.2 kHz). The frame lasts Tf = 1/8000 = 125 µs.
Coding. 8 bits per sample with A-law companding gives about 38 dB SQNR over a 40 dB range of talkers; each channel needs 8 × 8000 = 64 kbit/s.

Frame. Give every 8-bit unit its own slot: 30 speech slots, slot 0 for frame alignment and alarms, and slot 16 for signalling (dialled digits, on-hook and off-hook), 32 slots in all. Bits per frame = 32 × 8 = 256.
Rates and times.

Minimal alternative. A bare frame of 30 × 8 + 1 sync bit = 241 bits would run at 241 × 8000 = 1.928 Mbit/s, only 0.4 % overhead, but it has no signalling channel and a 1-bit sync that data can imitate. Note that 30 slots plus one sync slot gives 31 × 8 = 248 bits, 1.984 Mbit/s; 2.048 Mbit/s is not a rounding of that but the 32-slot frame.

Synchronization. Send a 7-bit frame alignment word (0011011 in E1) in slot 0 of alternate frames. A random 7-bit pattern matches it with probability 1/2⁷ = 1/128, so the receiver declares alignment only after the word appears in the right place in several successive frames, and declares loss only after several misses.

Timing and guard time. The receiver recovers the 2.048 MHz clock from the line signal with a PLL. With a recovered clock, the decision instant stays within a small fraction of the 0.488 µs bit, so no guard bits are needed; the line code must therefore guarantee transitions. Jitter accumulates along a chain of repeaters, so each repeater filters its clock.

Line code. Use HDB3: AMI (no DC, first null at Rb = 2.048 MHz, so it fits about the same band as NRZ) with every run of four 0s replaced by a pattern containing a deliberate bipolar violation, so the clock never starves and the receiver can still detect single errors.

Comparison with E1. The design is the E1 primary rate: 32 slots, 2.048 Mbit/s, slot 0 alignment, slot 16 signalling, A-law, HDB3. The North American T1 instead packs 24 slots plus 1 framing bit (193 bits, 1.544 Mbit/s) and steals signalling bits from speech slots in every sixth frame.
Closing check. 32 slots × 8 bits × 0.488 µs = 125 µs, one frame; and 30 × 64 + 128 = 2048 kbit/s.

glossary.def: Taking the values of a continuous signal at instants T<sub>s</sub> = 1/f<sub>s</sub> apart.
The lowest sampling rate, 2f<sub>m</sub>, that avoids aliasing for a signal bandlimited to f<sub>m</sub>.
f<sub>s</sub>/2, about which components above it fold down as aliases.
The gap f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>m</sub> between the baseband and the first spectral copy, where filters roll off.
PAM in which the pulse top follows the message during the pulse.
PAM in which each pulse is held at the sample value for τ; causes the aperture effect.
Droop of the message band by sinc(fτ) caused by holding samples; corrected by a 1/sinc equalizer.
τ/T<sub>s</sub>, the fraction of each period a pulse occupies.
The spacing Δ between neighbouring quantization levels.
The rounding error of a quantizer; Δ²/12 in power for a uniform quantizer.
V/σ, the ratio of the quantizer range to the rms signal; it sets the SQNR for a given n.
Clipping of samples beyond the quantizer range ±V.
A compressor at the transmitter and an expander at the receiver that together give non-uniform quantization.
Logarithmic companding law with μ = 255, used in North America and Japan.
Companding law, linear below 1/A and logarithmic above, with A = 87.6, used in Europe and India.
The n-bit binary number that stands for one quantized sample in PCM.
A unit that decides each received bit and sends a fresh pulse, so noise does not accumulate.
The SQNR improvement of DPCM over PCM, 10 log(σ²/σ<sub>e</sub>²).
The copy of the receiver inside a DPCM or DM transmitter that forms the reconstructed samples for prediction.
Delta-modulation distortion when the input changes faster than Δf<sub>s</sub>.
The ±Δ hunting of a delta-modulation staircase around a slow input.
Quantization noise heard when the input is silent.
One complete round of TDM slots, lasting 1/f<sub>s</sub>.
A fixed bit pattern by which a TDM receiver finds the start of each frame.
Leakage of one TDM channel into a neighbouring slot through timing error or pulse spreading.
Alternate mark inversion: a bipolar line code sending 0 as 0 V and 1s as alternate +V and −V.
A line code with a transition at the centre of every bit; DC-free and self-clocking.
The distribution of a signal’s power over frequency, in W/Hz.
